gaps: The field study did not assess anatomical morphology or diagnostic variation.
The field study does not assess reproduction, development, survival, or longevity.

claims.text: At Kalinzu Forest, the study followed one habituated family group for 4,308 hours between November 2013 and April 2016. The observed group devoted 87.0% of feeding time to young leaves, 9.8% to fruits, and smaller proportions to flowers, bark, soil, and unspecified foods. In fine-grained analyses of selected leaf items, crude protein content, digestibility, and toughness were associated with dietary choices; the evaluated factors did not explain whether specific leaf items were consumed at the broader eaten-versus-not-eaten level. These findings are limited to this group, site, methods, and study period.
claims.locator: Abstract ¶1; Materials and Methods > Study Site and Collection of Behavioral Data ¶¶2–5; Results > Dietary Choice ¶¶1–3 and Tables 3–4; Discussion > Selection Between Eaten and Not Eaten Leaves ¶1 / Selection Within the Eaten Leaves ¶1.
claims.placeTimeScope: Kalinzu Forest, western Uganda; behavioral observations November 2013–April 2016 (4,308 hours); one group, originally identified as 11 individuals. The claim concerns observed group-level feeding and study analyses, not a population-wide estimate.
claims.lifeStatus: Habituated, free-ranging wild animals; no captive or domesticated animals included.

gaps: Single-group evidence cannot establish species-wide dietary composition or generality across populations, seasons, and habitats.
This batch assessed one ecological facet from one primary study; interactions, broad habitat use, and other ecological dimensions remain unreviewed.
No phylogeny, divergence estimate, or comparative evolutionary analysis was assessed.
A single study location is not a reviewed current or historical range inventory.
No fossil occurrence or geological age evidence was assessed.
No formal conservation assessment, population trend, or risk category was reviewed.

reasons: Only one field study and one ecological facet were assessed; six facets remain not-assessed.
The one-group study cannot represent species-wide ecology or distribution.
No systematic literature search or independent expert review has been completed.
